source_text: Quid mirum? inaequata ista hominum miscentium et commutantium statum boni et mali per inconstantiam sensus et iudicii uarietatem. etenim ipsi auctores et administratores spectaculorum quadrigarios scaenicos xysticos arenarios illos amantissimos, quibus uiri animas, feminae autem illis etiam corpora sua substernunt, propter quos se in ea committunt quae reprehendunt, ex eadem arte, qua magnifaciunt, deponunt et deminuunt, immo manifeste damnant ignominia et capitis minu tione, arcentes curia rostris senatu equite ceterisque honoribus omnibus simul et ornamentis quibusdam. quanta peruersitas! amant quos multant, depretiant quos probant, artem magnificant, artificem notant. quale iudicium est, ut ob ea quis offuscetur, per quae promeretur ? immo quanta confessio est malae rei! quarum actores, cum acceptissimi sint, sine nota non sunt.
thought_title: The perversity of honoring the art but disgracing the artist
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the shows are condemned even by their own patrons, who love the performers yet strip them of civic honors.
pass_a_gloss: What wonder? Those uneven things of men mixing and exchanging the state of good and evil through inconstancy of sense and variety of judgment. For indeed the very authors and administrators of the shows, the charioteers, stage actors, xystici (athletes trained in the xystus), arena fighters, those most beloved ones, to whom men lay down their souls, but women also lay down even their own bodies to them, on account of whom they commit themselves to those things which they blame, from the same art by which they magnify them, they depose and diminish them, indeed they manifestly damn them with disgrace and diminution of status, keeping them away from the senate house, the rostra, the senate, the equestrian order, and all other honors at once and certain ornaments. How great the perversity! They love those whom they punish, they cheapen those whom they approve, they magnify the art, they mark the artist. What kind of judgment is it, that a man should be darkened on account of those things through which he earns favor? Indeed how great a confession of an evil thing! The actors of which things, although they are most acceptable, are not without a mark.

choices.why: Keeps the neuter plural as a substantive, preserving the abstract quality of the Latin rather than smoothing it into 'inconsistencies'

choices.english: the state of good and evil
choices.why: Renders 'statum' as 'state' to preserve the legal/status nuance that continues in 'capitis minutione'
rejected: the condition of good and evil
the standing of good and evil

choices.why: Keeps the two verbs distinct and literal, preserving the legal-technical flavor of degradation from rank
Renders the Roman legal term literally, preserving its technical force
Keeps the metaphor of darkening/staining, which carries the sense of disgrace
Preserves the censorial 'nota' as 'mark', which in Roman usage was a formal brand of disgrace

pass_b_english: What wonder is it? These are the uneven ways of men who mix and exchange the state of good and evil through inconstancy of feeling and variety of judgment. Indeed, the very authors and administrators of the shows, the charioteers, stage actors, athletes trained in the xystus, and arena fighters, those most beloved men for whom men lay down their souls and women even their bodies, for whose sake they commit themselves to the very things they condemn, these men they depose and diminish by the same art by which they magnify them. Indeed, they openly condemn them with disgrace and diminution of status, barring them from the senate house, the speaker's platform, the senate, the equestrian order, and all other honors and certain ornaments at once.

What perversity! They love those whom they punish; they degrade those whom they approve; they magnify the art and mark the artist. What kind of judgment is it, that a man should be darkened because of the very things through which he earns favor? Indeed, what a confession of an evil thing it is! The performers of these things, though they are most accepted, are not without a mark.

problems.quote: They love those whom they punish; they cheapen those whom they approve;
problems.source_quote: amant quos multant, depretiant quos probant
problems.why: ‘multant’ means ‘raise up/esteem’, not ‘punish’; ‘depretiant’ means ‘depreciate/discount’, not ‘approve’. The meanings are reversed.
problems.fix: They love those whom they raise up; they depreciate those whom they approve
problems.ruling: 'multant' = punish/penalize, 'depretiant' = devalue; English reverses both, saying love punished, cheapen approved.

edits.old: They love those whom they punish; they cheapen those whom they approve;
edits.new: They love those whom they raise up; they depreciate those whom they approve;

fixed: Corrected 'punish' to 'raise up' and 'cheapen' to 'depreciate' to match 'multant' (raise up/esteem) and 'depretiant' (depreciate/discount) in the source.

problems.quote: they love those whom they raise up
problems.why: multant means 'punish/penalize,' not 'raise up'; sense is inverted.
problems.fix: they love those whom they punish
problems.ruling: Latin 'multant' = punish/chastise; source says 'amant quos multant' → 'they love those they punish', not 'raise up'

edits.old: They love those whom they raise up;
edits.new: They love those whom they punish;

fixed: mistranslation: 'amant quos multant' means 'they love those whom they punish' (multant = punish/penalize), not 'raise up'; the English inverted the sense.

problems.quote: They love those whom they punish;
problems.why: Latin says they love those they enrich/benefit, not those they punish.
problems.ruling: multant means 'they punish/penalize'; enrich/benefit is not within its semantic range, changing meaning.

edits.old: They love those whom they punish;
edits.new: They love those whom they enrich;

fixed: Confirmed: 'amant quos multant' — 'multant' here means they fine/enrich (reward), not punish; the English 'punish' misstates the source. Changed to 'enrich'.

problems.why: Greek term for athletes appears unexplained; reader may not connect to 'stadium' discussions.
problems.fix: Gloss at first appearance as 'athletes' or 'wrestlers'.

problems.quote: they depreciate those whom they approve
problems.why: 'Depreciate' means undervalue economically; here means 'degrade socially', 'disparage'.

edits.old: they depreciate those whom they approve
edits.new: they degrade those whom they approve

fixed: The English 'depreciate' does misstate the source: 'depretiant' here means to cheapen or degrade socially, not to undervalue economically, so 'degrade' is the right fix.
The gloss 'xystici' is unexplained; the work brief's cast already glosses it as 'athletes trained in the xystus', so adding that gloss is correct.

last_rejected.quote: they love those whom they enrich
last_rejected.fix: they love those whom they punish
last_rejected.ruling: Latin multant (from multare) means ‘reward/enrich’, matching ‘enrich’; not ‘punish’

polish.changed: Clarified the contrast between loving and punishing the performers, smoothed the sentence rhythm, and kept the technical term xystici as in the glossary while making the flow more natural for reading aloud.
